Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

issues.explanation: For an 18-year-old male whose trauma type is rape, the trigger 'Military Topics' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other trigger, threat, and memory items coherently suggest interpersonal/close-contact danger (touch, strangers, shouting, doors, vivid sensory reliving), but military-related talk implies a trauma context that is otherwise absent. This is not supported by the threat or memory content and does not fit the formulation as a plausible trigger tightly linked to the presented threat-memory pattern.

vignette:
Kamau was 18, a single African American young man working as a tax consultant, and when he first came in for help he described feeling as though ordinary parts of his day had become laced with danger. The assault happened the previous year, when he was still trying to settle into adult routines and had begun working in an office where he met clients, answered questions at a front desk, and moved between small rooms with doors that opened and shut constantly. He had been raped by a man he had known only casually, after finding himself alone with him in a situation that had seemed ordinary at first and then suddenly unsafe. Kamau spoke about the event carefully, with a long silence between sentences, but what stood out most was how the experience was still present to him in fragments that arrived without warning. He did not describe a complete, organized memory so much as flashes: a picture of the room, the angle of a wall, the hard edges of the setting, and the sense that he was trapped in a moment he could not control. At times, he said, the memory came back not as an image at all but as the same overwhelming feeling that had come over him then, with no clear picture attached. When that happened, his body reacted before his mind could catch up, and he would feel sick with the same intensity as if the event were happening again. He also noticed that the taste from that time could return with the memory, vivid and immediate, as if his mouth had been pulled back into that moment.

In the months that followed, Kamau found that certain sounds could pull him sharply into alertness. Shouting made him tense instantly, especially if voices rose suddenly in the apartment complex or on the street near his office, because loud anger now seemed to him to signal that something was about to go wrong. Doors opening or slamming had a similar effect; the sudden bang of a conference room door at work, or the front door of the building closing hard behind a client, could make him jump and turn before he had even registered what he was hearing. He was especially uneasy around men when he was alone with them. Even when nothing overtly threatening was happening, he watched their movements closely and calculated how quickly he could leave. He said that being approached by strangers in ordinary settings felt threatening, not because he believed every person meant to harm him, but because he no longer trusted himself to assess danger quickly enough once someone was close. That uncertainty left him uneasy in places he did not know, and he began avoiding unfamiliar locations whenever he could. He would rather take a longer route he knew well than enter a new building, new block, or new office where he could not tell what the exits were or who might be inside.

At work, these reactions quietly altered the way he moved through the day. The tax consulting office was full of doors, client interruptions, and the kind of quick exchanges that could not always be predicted. Kamau learned to choose the chair closest to the exit and to keep his attention split between his work and the sounds in the hallway. If a colleague approached too quickly and touched his shoulder from behind, he reacted with alarm that he found embarrassing but could not stop. He would flinch and step away, his heart racing, and then spend the next few minutes trying to look composed. Over time, he became more selective about assignments that would take him to unfamiliar client sites, saying he had other obligations or preferring to work from the office instead. Even in his neighborhood, he planned routes around places he did not know, and the limits of those choices began to narrow his world. Friends noticed that he declined invitations more often, especially if they involved meeting new people or going somewhere he had not been before.

By the time he sought help, Kamau was exhausted by the effort of staying on guard. He said he was not coming because he believed anything had "fixed itself" with time, but because he was tired of reacting so strongly to things other people seemed to brush off - a shouted argument, a slamming door, an unexpected hand on his shoulder, a man standing too close. He wanted to feel less threatened in ordinary places and to be able to work without constantly scanning for danger. What frightened him most was the sense that he could never fully tell when he was safe, and what he hoped for was not to forget what had happened, but to be able to live without the event breaking into the present so violently and so often.
